passage: In the office pantry after the quarterly review, Mohit found Sudha standing with her back to the room, wiping her eyes with her dupatta. He stopped in the doorway. He couldn't tell whether it was the review, something at home, or a message from her family. He said quietly, "Do you want company, or should I leave you be?" Sudha gave a wet laugh. "Stay if you like. It's good news, actually. I got the promotion, and my father would have loved to hear it." She kept crying, and Mohit filled a glass of water and set it beside her without saying anything. After a while she said, "Thanks for not guessing." He said, "I nearly did."

qa.q: What did Mohit ask Sudha in the pantry?
qa.a: He asked whether she wanted company or should he leave her be.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling as she cried?
qa.a: Mixed feelings, glad about the promotion and sad that her father cannot hear it; the tears alone could not have told Mohit which.

qa.q: What did Mohit do that respected Sudha?
qa.a: He asked instead of guessing, offered the choice of company or privacy, and brought water.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt before he asked?
qa.a: Uncertain, since he did not know whether the tears were about the review or about home.

grounding: A young adult cries from mixed feelings at work, and a colleague asks and offers privacy instead of guessing the cause from the tears.

passage:
Subject: About this morning

Dear Preeti,
I wanted to write because I left the meeting so quickly. I got tearful when the client shouted about the delay, and I didn't want to fall apart in front of everyone. It wasn't only the shouting. I've slept badly for a week and my grandmother is unwell, so it all came out at once. I'm okay now, just tired. Thank you for pausing the call and asking if I wanted water. I appreciated that you didn't ask me to explain there. If it's alright, I'd like fifteen minutes with you tomorrow to go through what the client actually needs.

Jagdish

qa.q: What did Preeti offer during the call?
qa.a: Preeti paused the call and asked if Jagdish wanted water.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling in the meeting, and what else was behind it?
qa.a: Jagdish felt upset and overwhelmed, getting tearful when the client shouted; a week of poor sleep and a grandmother being unwell were also behind it.

qa.q: What could Preeti reply to Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti can say it is good to hear Jagdish is okay, agree to the fifteen minutes and offer support if Jagdish needs time.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt seeing Jagdish tearful?
qa.a: Concerned, and perhaps unsure how to help; pausing the call and offering water shows care without pushing.

grounding: A young adult who was tearful at work explains that the cause was mixed, since tears alone do not show it, and appreciates a colleague who gave privacy.

passage: Aparna, you asked what happened at the office on Tuesday. So. I opened the email at my desk, and my UK visa had finally come through, after eleven months and two refusals. And I just burst into tears. Proper tears, shoulders shaking. Within a minute, three people were around my desk. One was patting my back, saying, "It's okay, there'll be other chances." Another brought water and asked if someone had died. I couldn't even speak. Then Neha from accounts crouched down, not touching me, and asked quietly, "Good tears or bad tears? And do you want the meeting room to yourself?" I laughed through it, nodded, and said, "Good. Very good. Room, please." She walked me there and shut the door. I cried for ten minutes, called my mother, and came out grinning. So that's what I, Sabina, learned that day: tears don't come with labels. Ask, and give people a door.

qa.q: How long had Sabina waited for the visa?
qa.a: Eleven months.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she burst into tears?
qa.a: Sabina was overwhelmed with relief and joy after months of waiting and two refusals, not sad as the colleagues assumed.

qa.q: Why was Neha's response the most helpful?
qa.a: Neha asked what kind of tears they were instead of assuming, didn't touch without asking, and offered privacy in the meeting room.

qa.q: How did the first colleagues read Sabina's tears?
qa.a: They assumed bad news, one offering comfort about other chances and another asking if someone had died.

grounding: A young adult describes crying with relief at work, colleagues assuming grief, and one colleague asking and offering privacy.

passage: I'm Yash, and I sit beside Sachin in the planning team. At Friday's meeting our director announced that Mr. Kapur, who'd trained half of us, was "taking early retirement". The director smiled and said it was his choice. I glanced at Sachin. His jaw was clenched, and his eyes were full of tears he wasn't letting fall. I couldn't tell what they meant. Sadness at losing his mentor? Something else? After the meeting he went straight to the stairwell. I waited ten minutes, then took him a cup of tea and stood a little distance away. "Do you want company, or should I leave you be?" He took the tea. "Company's fine." Then, quietly: "It wasn't his choice. They pushed him out. I'm not sad. I'm angry." I nodded. I'd assumed grief. I asked if he wanted to talk to HR about how it was handled, or just let off steam first. "Steam first," he said. "Then HR."

qa.q: What did the director announce about Mr. Kapur?
qa.a: That he was taking early retirement.

qa.q: What was Sachin really feeling behind the tears?
qa.a: Sachin was angry, not only sad, believing Mr. Kapur had been pushed out rather than choosing to leave.

qa.q: How did Yash offer support without assuming?
qa.a: Yash waited, brought tea, kept a little distance, asked whether Sachin wanted company or space, and then asked what Sachin wanted to do next.

qa.q: How had Yash read the tears at first?
qa.a: Yash assumed they were tears of grief at losing a mentor, and learned they were anger.

grounding: An observer describes a colleague's held-back tears, assumes grief, and learns by asking that they came from anger.

Wednesday: Vikas stopped at Ojas's desk in the morning. "Thanks for yesterday. It's my dog. Bruno. Fourteen years. He died on Sunday." His voice wobbled. "Everyone thinks I'm just exhausted." qa.a: Fourteen years.

passage: You looked worried when you saw me dab my eyes at the retirement lunch, Irfan. Sit, I'll tell you something. I'm Manjula, thirty years in this accounts office, and at twenty-five I cried at this very desk. My father's surgery had gone well that morning; the call came at eleven, after a week of night shifts at the hospital. The relief just spilled out. Mr Bhalla from audit walked past, saw my face and marched to our manager to complain that someone had been harsh with me. Only Lakshmi from payroll came over, set down a cup of tea and asked, "Good tears or bad ones? Do you want company, or shall I shut the door?" I said, "Good. Door, please." She closed it and left me alone for ten minutes. Today at the lunch, my tears were gratitude and a little grief at leaving. You couldn't have known that by looking, so thank you for asking me instead of guessing.

qa.q: What news came at eleven on the day Manjula cried at the desk?
qa.a: The call said Manjula's father's surgery had gone well that morning.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when the tears came at twenty-five, and how else were they read?
qa.a: Manjula felt deep relief after a week of fear and tiring night shifts, so they were good tears; Mr Bhalla read the same tears as hurt from a harsh manager.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped most, and why?
qa.a: Lakshmi's question helped most: she asked what kind of tears they were and offered company or a shut door, so Manjula could choose instead of being guessed about.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt about Mr Bhalla's complaint, and what would have changed if he had asked first?
qa.a: The manager may have felt accused of something they never did; if Mr Bhalla had asked Manjula first, he would have learned the tears were relief and skipped the complaint.

grounding: Shows that a young adult's tears at work can come from relief rather than hurt, and that asking and offering privacy is more respectful than guessing.
